Q: Is there a simple elegant way to convert a String to a Set of Characters in Java? A:

Beware: The char type (and its wrapper class Character) has been essentially broken since Java 2, and legacy since Java 5. As a 16-bit value, char is physically incapable of representing most characters.

Instead of char, use code point integer numbers when working with individual characters. Every one of the 159,801 characters defined in Unicode has been permanently assigned a code point number in the range of 0 to 1,114,111.

You can easily generate a stream of code points for the characters in a string. From there map each code point back to text, text containing a single character. Collect into a list.

Here is some untested code.

List < String > hexDigits =
    "0123456789ABCDEFabcdef"
        .codePoints()
        .map( Character :: toString )
        .toList() ;

You asked for an unmodifiable Set. Just use Set.copyOf for that.

Set < String > hexDigitsSet = Set.copyOf( hexDigits );

Perhaps you want those characters kept in your original order with a SequencedSet. Use a concrete class such as LinkedHashSet to preserve insertion-order.

SortedSet < String > hexDigits =
    "0123456789ABCDEFabcdef"
        .codePoints()
        .map( Character :: toString )
        .collect(
            Collectors.toCollection( LinkedHashSet :: new )
        );

Or, perhaps you want those characters kept in alphabetical order. Use a concrete class such as TreeSet for natural-order.

SortedSet < String > hexDigits =
    "0123456789ABCDEFabcdef"
        .codePoints()
        .map( Character :: toString )
        .collect(
            Collectors.toCollection( TreeSet :: new )
        );

You can make either SequencedSet unmodifiable.

SequencedSet < String > unmodifiableHexDigits = Collections.unmodifiableSequencedSet( hexDigits ) ;

Be aware that the approach described here only works for simple text. Some of what you might perceive as single characters is actually composed of multiple code points. For example, diacriticals (accent marks).

Q: How do I create an admin panel using React, Node.js with Express, and PostgreSQL? A:

sorry, i misundertood the question, when the frontend sends information to the backend, it does it through an HTTP request containing structured data, usually in JSON format, the backend receives this request and immediately assumes the data could be incorrect or malicious, so it validates that the data is complete, properly formatted, and appropriate for that specific request. If the request is for login or sign-up, the server verifies the credentials, applies security rules, and decides whether the action should succeed or fail. If it succeeds, the backend performs the actual work by communicating with the database to read or write data, applying business logic, and enforcing permissions such as admin-only actions. Once processing is finished, the backend sends an HTTP response back to the frontend, and the frontend simply displays the result to the user, you can read more here https://www.bezkoder.com/react-node-express-postgresql/

Q: What are the minimum and maximum escape numbers supported in the regular expression? A:

In Python regular expressions, escape sequences like \123 refer to octal values. The valid range for octal escape sequences is \0 to \377 (octal), which corresponds to character codes 0 to 255. For values larger than \777, you'll need to use Unicode escapes, like \u for 4-digit or \U for 8-digit Unicode values.

In your example, \1234 and \567890 are invalid because they exceed the allowed octal range. You can either split them into smaller valid octal numbers or use Unicode escapes if necessary.

Q: Nodejs - TypeError: logger.info is not a function A:

You're exporting a Morgan instance (which is a middleware function), not a Winston logger instance. Therefore, the object that you get from require('./logger') is not a Logger, and it doesn't have an .info() method.

You should export a logger instead, and wrap it in Morgan only for passing to app.use().
